name: Real-Time Communication
intent: Pick how a server tells a client that something happened: by the client asking repeatedly (polling), by holding a request open (long polling), or by keeping a connection open for pushes (server-sent events and WebSockets).
scenario: A live dashboard, a chat window and a stock ticker all need updates the moment they happen. HTTP was designed so that a client asks and a server answers, so pushing needs a technique.
problem: Plain HTTP only lets the client start a conversation. To show new data promptly, the client must either keep asking (wasting requests and adding delay) or the connection must stay open so that the server can speak first. Each approach costs different amounts of server resources, latency and complexity.

howItWorks.title: Short polling: ask every few seconds
howItWorks.text: The client sends a request on a timer and the server answers immediately, with data or 'nothing new'. It is the simplest and works through every proxy. Most requests are empty, and updates are late by up to the polling interval, so you pay a lot for freshness.

howItWorks.title: Long polling: ask and wait
howItWorks.text: The client sends a request and the server holds it open until there is something to say (or a timeout), then answers and the client asks again straight away. Updates arrive almost instantly with ordinary HTTP, but each update costs a full request cycle and every client holds a connection open.

howItWorks.title: Server-sent events (SSE): a one-way stream
howItWorks.text: The client opens one HTTP request and the server keeps it open, sending a stream of events down it. Browsers reconnect automatically and resume from the last event id. It is simple, efficient and ideal when only the server talks: notifications, live scores, progress.

howItWorks.title: WebSocket: a two-way connection
howItWorks.text: An HTTP request is upgraded into a persistent two-way channel, and either side can send messages at any time with very little overhead. It is the right tool for chat, collaboration and games, at the cost of stateful servers and some extra work for scaling, authentication and reconnecting.

howItWorks.title: Plan for reconnection and scale
howItWorks.text: Connections drop. Clients must reconnect with backoff and jitter, and resume from where they left off using an id or sequence number. Servers holding many open connections need to be sized by connections, not requests, and need a way to route a message to whichever server holds the recipient's connection.

pros: Push techniques deliver updates in milliseconds, not seconds
SSE and WebSocket avoid thousands of empty requests
Long polling and SSE work over ordinary HTTP infrastructure
WebSocket supports true two-way, low-overhead messaging
cons: Open connections consume memory and sockets on servers and proxies
Stateful connections complicate load balancing, deploys and scaling out
Some proxies and networks interfere with long-lived connections
Reconnection, ordering and missed-message recovery must be designed
whenToUse: Short polling for infrequent, low-stakes updates, where simplicity matters most
WebSocket for chat, collaboration, multiplayer and anything bidirectional
whenNotToUse: Polling every second for thousands of users, which turns into a denial-of-service on yourself
WebSocket for data that changes once an hour
Any push technique without a way to catch up after a disconnect
pitfalls: No heartbeat, so dead connections linger and users appear online forever
A reconnect storm when a server restarts and everyone returns at once
Sending updates without ids, so a reconnecting client cannot tell what it missed
Forgetting authentication and authorization on the long-lived connection
